items.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998
items.q: my friend Dan Morgenstern and his friend David Himmelstein, they got to the Little Theater in New York... And we were talking afterwards and they said, about whom they should have next, and I said well why don’t you get Earl Hines

ctx.x: Was there a difference in sound, to your ears, between most of the white bands and most of the black big bands?

Yes. Yes. I think so. I think in a sense, and you might say in the early days, the white bands were a bit more polished, but they didn’t swing. You know, that was really, I mean when Basie’s band comes out of Kansas City and there’s a sensation, George Simon, the critic said it was out of tune and everything. And well they were playing with instruments which were battered, had rubber bands and chewing gum on them, that sort of thing. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

of course a lot of those musicians didn’t have the education that white musicians had had. They were probably not good readers to start with. So that was why Basie’s thing stressed head arrangements, which they sort of cooked up themselves. But you know if you take the best black bands of the swing era, from the point of swinging they are undoubtedly very much superior. But you can take Goodman’s band, it’s probably the best of the white bands, Artie Shaw’s, Glenn Miller’s, Tommy Dorsey had a very good band. But…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: my old friend Stanley Dance, who had by then settled in the U.S. ... We called Earl. We had Stanley Dance help us. Stanley was all for this. ... Stanley later on thought, like some people will with the passing of time, that it had been his idea, which it was not. It was our idea, but we enlisted him

ctx.x: We were going to pick up with your enrolling in Brandeis without your knowledge.

I came in the middle of the academic year. I had gotten out of the Army in January. So right after the winter break I arrived at Brandeis. It was very small then. The first class had just graduated. That was the class of 1952. They had just graduated the previous fall. It was still very small, about 700 undergraduate students, and a great faculty. I quickly made some friends. I was older. I’m 24 now, right? Yes, I’m 24. Of course that was a little more than the average age certainly of incoming freshmen, but…

There was no jazz instruction at Brandeis, needless to say. It had a very good music department, with an all-star faculty of Harold Shapiro and the very gifted, excellent composer, who died very young, named Irving Fine. The titular was Leonard Bernstein, who came in once a week. He was known as the airborne professor, because he flew in from New York to give a lecture which was attended by practically everybody, because he was a brilliant lecturer. We decided – this small core of jazz fans – that since there was…
